posts.cooked:
I run a small dropshipping store and built an automation that syncs supplier stock to Shopify every 4 hours. It works, but I still worry about the gap: an item can sell out at the supplier between syncs and a customer can still order it.

For those of you with supplier-based inventory:

  • How often do you sync?
  • Do you keep a safety buffer (for example, showing 0 when the supplier has fewer than 5)?
  • How do you handle the occasional order for something that’s actually gone?

Curious what’s worked for others.

I’d set the buffer by how fast each item sells rather than one number for the whole catalog. For slow items, showing 0 once the supplier is down to 2 or 3 is plenty. For your top sellers, sync those more often if the supplier’s feed allows it, and use a bigger buffer. Push the supplier quantity minus the buffer into Shopify, and make sure “Continue selling when out of stock” is off on those variants so checkout stops at 0.

For the order that slips through anyway, email the customer the same day: give a real ship date if the supplier is restocking soon, or cancel it from the order page, where the Cancel order dialog lets you refund and restock in one step.

Four hours is not a bad interval on its own, and I would look at the feed before I tried to sync more often. Most of the oversells I have seen came from the spreadsheet behind the sync, not the timing. Raw supplier counts had duplicate SKUs, SKUs that did not quite match the Shopify variant, and rows where stock fell sharply between one file and the next, and all of that went straight into the store because the import trusted it.

What helps is a quick cleanup pass before anything is pushed live. Keep the supplier quantity in one column, work out the quantity you actually want Shopify to show in another, and hold back the odd rows for a manual look instead of importing them automatically. A sharp drop, a missing SKU, or a product that suddenly reappears after being gone is worth checking, because no sync schedule can fix a bad row, it just publishes it faster. I spend a lot of time on this kind of supplier file cleanup at https://runeloresupply.com, and once that exception check is routine, a four-hour sync feels a lot safer.

When one still slips through, checking that held-back list first also makes the customer message easier, because you know whether it was a genuine sell-out or a feed mistake. You can then contact them the same day with a confirmed restock date, a sensible alternative, or a refund, rather than a vague apology while you try to work out what happened.

Thanks, this is really helpful. Setting the buffer by how fast each item sells makes a lot more sense than one number for everything. I’ll try a small buffer for slow items and a bigger one with more frequent syncs for my best sellers. Good reminder on “Continue selling when out of stock” too. I’ll double-check it’s off on all variants.

Thanks, that’s a great point. Bad data does more damage than slow timing. I already validate SKUs and variant IDs before anything gets written to Shopify, but I like the idea of flagging sharp stock drops and products that suddenly reappear for a manual check instead of pushing them live. Adding that to my sync.

Hey @mrbasitafg

After each sync, check Products > Inventory in the admin for negative quantities. Those are the oversells, because the sync wrote the supplier’s 0 onto a variant that had already sold. Sorting by inventory shows them quickly and gives you a real oversell rate instead of a worry.

If one fast mover keeps landing negative, sync just that item more often or pull it from the store.

When an order does slip through, cancel and refund it the same day rather than waiting to see if the supplier restocks. Customers take that much better than a delayed “sorry, it’s gone”.

ai_summary.summarized_text:
A small dropshipping store syncs supplier inventory to Shopify every four hours, but worries that products may sell out between updates and still be ordered. The discussion suggests that four hours can be reasonable; feed accuracy and item-specific safeguards matter as much as sync frequency.

Recommended practices include setting safety buffers based on how quickly each product sells, using larger buffers and more frequent updates for top sellers, and turning off “Continue selling when out of stock” on variants. Before importing supplier data, validate SKUs and variant IDs and manually review missing items, sharp stock drops, and products that suddenly reappear.

After each sync, checking Shopify inventory for negative quantities can reveal oversells and help identify products that need faster updates or removal. If an order cannot be fulfilled, contact the customer promptly with a confirmed restock date or alternative, or cancel and refund it. The store owner plans to adopt these measures; no outcome has yet been reported.
